# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting close to red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach temperatures hot enough to vaporize rock on close-orbiting worlds, while the nightside plunges to hundreds of degrees below zero, potentially freezing atmospheres onto the surface. On planets like the real-world example 55 Cancri e, dayside temperatures exceed 2,000°C.

However, atmosphere and oceans can moderate these extremes. Winds transport heat from the dayside to the nightside, and climate models suggest that a sufficiently dense atmosphere—perhaps a few bars of CO₂—could keep temperatures habitable across the entire surface. Ocean worlds benefit even more, as water's high heat capacity makes it an exceptional heat transporter.

The climate of a tidally locked world would be strikingly static yet dynamic. With no day-night cycle, weather patterns become fixed: permanent storms at the terminator (the boundary between day and night), constant upwelling on the dayside, and steady winds flowing between hemispheres.
